title: Cross-Platform Online Team Formation in Spatial Crowdsourcing

problem.claim: Spatial crowdsourcing needs online teams with multiple skills for increasingly complex tasks.

gap.claim: Single-platform team formation limits skill diversity, while cross-platform cooperation must address localized raw data and additional cooperation costs.

contributions.claim: Defines the Cross-platform Online Team Formation (COTF) problem.
Proposes a COTF framework and Random Cooperation Strategy.
Proposes PQROS for adaptive-range-query worker selection and DQO for cost-effective scheduling using predictive revenue modeling.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that extensive experiments on real and synthetic datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed methods.

narrative_sequence.summary: Spatial crowdsourcing traditionally handles one-to-one services with single skills, while complex societal needs require multi-skill teams.
Single-platform methods restrict skill diversity, and cross-platform cooperation introduces data-localization and cooperation-cost challenges.
The paper defines COTF and proposes a framework with a Random Cooperation Strategy.
PQROS supports worker selection through adaptive range queries, while DQO supports cost-effective scheduling through predictive revenue modeling.
Experiments on real and synthetic datasets are reported to validate the methods' effectiveness.

source_observation.claim: Cross-platform cooperation is presented as a way to address limited skill diversity in single-platform team formation.

interpretation.claim: Broadening the worker pool can improve team skill coverage, but introduces privacy and coordination constraints.

application.claim: Design multi-platform team formation around localized data access and explicit cooperation-cost optimization.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish that cross-platform cooperation is preferable when tasks do not require multiple skills or when cooperation costs outweigh diversity benefits.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the algorithms' formal objectives, constraints, or complexity.
The abstract does not provide dataset sizes, baselines, quantitative results, or details of compliance with data protection regulations.
